artworks.title: Soft Power, AKA Venice in the Middle
artworks.descriptionShort: Transfer painting built from a failed Oslo canvas — the exact size requested for a Berlin group show. Multiple acrylic transfers are layered: a faded Oslo cityscape, a Rietveld-era painting using 2007 Venice Biennale photographs, a 1906 San Francisco earthquake aerial, and leftover WWII source photographs — held together with assertive colour fields.
artworks.intent: To use a failed transfer canvas as an opportunity to experiment — layering transfers from past paintings and pushing the painted color fields to dominate rather than support the photographic source material. The question was whether composition could be worked out through paint around a set of pre-existing image elements.

artworks.title: World War Two
artworks.intent: A painting examining how the recording medium doesn't just document war but actively manufactures the moral narrative attached to it — using color photography (WWII's dominant recording medium, versus WWI's black-and-white) and a central quoted image (the Khaldei Reichstag flag photograph) known to be staged and darkroom-edited.

artworks.title: World War One
artworks.intent: This is a painting about medium hidden in the fog of war — using the physical density and chaos of compositing dozens of photographs to make the recording medium itself, not just the war it depicts, the subject.

artworks.title: Almadinat Alearabia
artworks.descriptionShort: A satellite-imagery collage merging nine Arab League cities — Cairo, Baghdad, Riyadh, Amman, Algiers, Casablanca, Dubai, Damascus, Beirut — into one continuous urban geography.
artworks.intent: Made to connect with the Pallasseum's mixed community — German, Turkish, Arab, ex-Yugoslav residents — by giving each group a satellite-view portrait built from their own homeland cities, displayed full-size in their own courtyard.

artworks.title: Deutsche Stadt
artworks.descriptionShort: A seamless collage of satellite images of Germany's nine largest cities by population — Berlin, Hamburg, Munich, Frankfurt am Main, Cologne, Düsseldorf, Essen, Dortmund, and Stuttgart — stitched into a single continuous urban landscape. At first encounter it reads as one place; the collage only reveals itself on closer looking.
artworks.intent: To make a portrait of a country at the scale of its largest cities. Satellite imagery flattens urban space into a shared visual grammar — streets, houses, train tracks, rivers look fundamentally similar everywhere. The country framework reintroduces specificity within that sameness: you can see the uniqueness of a place precisely because the visual language is universal. The work operates at the threshold where settlement pattern becomes legible as national character.
artworks.primaryImageAltText: Deutsche Stadt, 2020. Seamless satellite image collage of Germany's nine largest cities by population, printed on aluminium mount, 140 × 200 cm.

artworks.title: San Francisco City 1906
artworks.intent: Uses the century-long gap between the source photograph and the painting to make a wider argument: that beauty and horror aren't opposites, only separated by time; that Lawrence himself was likely more captivated by the new aerial vantage point than by the disaster it happened to record; and, ultimately, a holistic view onto the human condition on this planet rather than a record of one city's tragedy.

artworks.title: Brandenburger Tor. 1899
artworks.descriptionShort: A 1899 photograph of the Brandenburg Gate, looking west along the walkway, transferred onto canvas and painted with flat acrylic colour fields — the first painting in the Gates of Perception series, and the originating work of Bernard Bolter's Berlin practice.
artworks.intent: To begin mapping the locations of the original Berlin customs wall gates — the Akzisemauer — starting with the Brandenburg Gate, the only one still standing. The discovery that the customs wall gates overlapped with the Cold War wall, and that many U-Bahn stations still carry the names of those gates (Kottbusser Tor, Hallesches Tor), made the subject feel alive and present rather than purely historical. The series emerged from wanting to see the Cold War wall in a longer timeline — one that preceded it and continued after it.
artworks.primaryImageAltText: Brandenburger Tor. 1899, 2017. Acrylic gel medium transfer and acrylic paint on canvas, 80 × 80 cm. Berlin.

artworks.title: Baker Beach . 1935
artworks.descriptionShort: Two fishermen cast lines at Baker Beach as the Golden Gate Bridge rises unfinished behind them, San Francisco, 2016.
artworks.intent: Painted at the point where the classical photo-transfer-plus-painted-field technique was reaching a natural, fluent finish — the last body of work made before the deliberate deconstruction of process that began after the move to Berlin. The bridge, visible from the artist's childhood home at 22nd Avenue and Fulton in San Francisco, functions as a personal icon rather than a found subject; the fishermen were included for the contrast between an ordinary, unhurried ritual and a landmark feat of engineering being born in the background — a moment of daily life the artist says he never once witnessed happening in his own life.

artworks.title: Cliff House . 1902
artworks.intent: To take a well-known, mass-produced, unauthored tourist photograph and run it through a deliberately personal, authored color process — testing the same warm/cool complementary color-balance principle (drawn originally from Goethe's Zur Farbenlehre, via Color Theory, 1995) against a subject far more iconic than the series' obscure founding image.

artworks.title: Golden Gate Bridge . 1935
artworks.mediumOther: t-shirt transfer and acrylic on canvas

artworks.title: Telegraph Hill .1868
artworks.mediumOther: t-shirt transfer and acrylic on canvas

artworks.title: Cliff House . 1863
artworks.descriptionShort: The first painting in the A Colorful History series. A t-shirt transfer of an 1863 photograph of the original Cliff House onto a 16 × 16 inch canvas, with flat acrylic colour fields in warm yellow, muted green, and soft blue-grey. Made in San Francisco in 2014, in response to conversations about how much the city had changed.
artworks.intent: Returned to San Francisco after seven years in Amsterdam and found the city deep in conversation about how much it had changed. That prompted a longer view — how has the city changed over the last 100 or 150 years? Using historical photographs to extend the timeline, viewing contemporary change from a much longer lens.

artworks.title: How to Euro Art School: Episode One
artworks.descriptionShort: A four-minute video monologue in which Bernard Bolter recalls the 1998 preliminary entrance exam at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie in Amsterdam — the act of making a painting to destroy it in the room as proof of readiness to start over.
artworks.intent: Conceived as the first in a planned series of videos tracing the artist's path to European art school. Episode One covers the origin — the 1998 preliminary entrance exam at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie in Amsterdam — as the logical starting point for the story. Further episodes were planned but not yet made.

artworks.title: Venice Biennale 2007
artworks.intent: The artist's later reflection on the piece: a figure on the inside trying to make sense of the inside, while yearning for the outside. Reflects real ambivalence about the high-art world at the time — engaged enough to build a whole composition around it, but never fully absorbed into it.

artworks.title: Skulptur Projekte Münster 2007
artworks.descriptionShort: A transfer painting made at the Gerrit Rietveld Akademie in 2007, combining multiple photographs from Skulptur Projekte Münster into a single landscape composition. The first work in Bolter's practice to layer multiple photo transfers on one canvas, bridging the Vanishing Landscapes series toward the conceptual ambition of what would become A Colorful History.
artworks.intent: To test whether the experience of a large-scale sculpture festival could be compressed into a single canvas using multiple photo transfers — to see how that would look and what it could hold.

artworks.title: Centraal Station Boats
artworks.intent: Not consciously about the vanishing Dutch landscape at the time of making. The mountain graphic breaking out of the billboard frame was a private, half-ironic response to the flatness of the Dutch landscape after a lifetime around San Francisco's hills — homesickness disguised as advertising. The 'vanishing landscape' reading only became legible in hindsight, decades later.

artworks.title: BASEL switzerland
artworks.descriptionShort: A seamless digital composite of Basel, Switzerland — the founding work of the Digital City Series. Four scenes captured on skateboard across the city's Altstadt are stitched into a single square composition, with the Rathaus and cathedral visible against an autumn palette. All hand-assembled in Photoshop, printed on aluminium at 48 × 48 inches.
artworks.intent: The square format was chosen because the work functions simultaneously as a portrait and a landscape — the only format that is both, or neither, refusing to choose between orientations. More fundamentally, the work is a portrait of a city as seen through the movement of a skateboard ride — cityscape landscapes assembled into a single portrait. The skateboard is the instrument of perception; the composition is what that movement produces.
artworks.primaryImageAltText: Basel Switzerland, 2007. Seamless digital composite printed on aluminium, 48 × 48 in. Digital City Series.

artworks.title: South Elliott and Lafayette
artworks.descriptionShort: Transfer painting of South Elliott and Lafayette Streets, Fort Greene, Brooklyn, fall 2004. Personal photograph on canvas via t-shirt transfer paper, with flat acrylic colour fields — painted sky above, buildings right, light post left. The corner's bulletproof bodega is long gone. A painting with a photo on it that doesn't exist anymore.
artworks.intent: The large sky was a recurring theme across the Brooklyn mini-series. The sky gives gravity to the image and creates space that plays against the detail of the photograph below.

artworks.title: Four Corners
artworks.intent: To translate an outer-borough, infrastructural view of New York -- Queens warehouses with Manhattan reduced to a distant background presence -- into a painting that ultimately became a fully invented, hand-painted cosmology. The squares (sun, moon, Mars, star) were not planned as symbolic content from the outset; they arrived while painting, after the swatch device in Transition and the checkerboard in Four Nations had already been worked out, and the sacred-four color palette of the Native American Church (white, red, black, yellow) is echoed loosely rather than deliberately -- Mars-as-red the one conscious anchor, black relocated from a checkerboard-equal color to the entire field of the sky.

artworks.title: Four Nations
artworks.descriptionShort: A photo-composite lower-Manhattan skyline -- Manhattan Bridge at left, an unidentified tower piercing a hand-painted sky at right -- fronted by an undulating, hand-painted checkerboard in white, red, black, and yellow across a rooftop parking lot. Third of the four original Art Collision compositions.
artworks.intent: The checkerboard was not planned as a symbolic device. The printed photo composite did not cover the full canvas, leaving open space at the artist's discretion; the checkerboard emerged as a formal response to that empty space. Only after arriving at the checkerboard did its four-color palette register as a direct reference to the four sacred colors of the Native American Church -- a meaning that attached itself after the formal decision, not before. This form-first, meaning-following sequence is confirmed by the artist as typical of the first four Art Collision paintings specifically.

artworks.title: Transition
artworks.descriptionShort: A photo-collaged composite Manhattan skyscraper framed by a hand-painted grey sky, flanked at its base by RGB and CMYK color swatches. Second of the four original Art Collision compositions, and the artist's first sustained use of photography in the work.
artworks.intent: Mainly the color switch, but it's also a transition for my style and the first use of photographs that continues in my works. I still thought of myself as a painter -- that's really why the photograph needed paint on it, not just a concept about print versus screen. It was also the first series I made after Utrecht, and in a real sense it was made against that experience -- not against art school as an idea, but against the specific version of it I found there: a concept-based program where the teachers used 'concept-based' as cover for not teaching technique, and behind it, a whole European system built around getting government subsidy to make art. I saw how that worked in practice -- shows staged less for a public and more to be photographed as proof that the funded work had actually happened. Art Collision, starting with this painting, was made deliberately outside that: DIY, self-organized shows with other artists in New York and a few spaces I'd kept in touch with in Holland, made to be seen rather than to be documented as compliant.

artworks.title: Prophecy
artworks.descriptionShort: A digital print and acrylic collage on canvas depicting the New York skyline as a tree growing from the earth, with painted housing project pairs extending to the left — a visual translation of the Hopi prophecy, in which one figure grows and disappears. The first work in the Art Collision series, made in Fort Greene, Brooklyn, in 2002.
artworks.intent: To translate the Hopi prophecy — a cave painting of two figures, one growing larger then disappearing — into a visual language rooted in the urban landscape of New York. The city becomes the organism: a tree growing from the earth, its skyline the canopy. The prophecy structure was not illustrated top-down but discovered within the source material during making.

artworks.title: Cardboardman Visits Utrecht
artworks.mediumOther: Cardboard box suit, street performance, documented with black-and-white photographs
artworks.descriptionShort: A collaborative street performance made with Jur Jarring at the HKU Utrecht in 2000. Dressed in a homemade cardboard box suit, the two artists walked from the art school into the centre of Utrecht and back — documented in three black-and-white photographs showing the suit progressively falling apart.
artworks.intent: The 2D photographs were the stated end goal of the assignment — the suit was a means to produce them, not an object to be presented in itself. Not much time was spent on the suit's construction; the walk and the documentation were the work.
artworks.primaryImageAltText: Utrecht, Netherlands, 2000. Black-and-white documentation photograph of a figure in a cardboard box suit walking along a Dutch brick street.

artworks.title: Mokum Straat
artworks.descriptionShort: A small pen drawing made on location in Amsterdam, circa 1997–98, during Bolter's first solo travels through Europe. Canal street scene with loose mark-making, one-line figures, and reinforced perspective lines — drawn from a canal bench, before any formal art training.

artworks.title: Education
artworks.descriptionShort: What is the 'birth of civilization' if not everything.
artworks.intent: The title is the thesis, not a neutral label: what a classical education teaches you to revere (the tower, rendered through the same fisheye/pedestal distortion used for elevated-but-unreachable subjects in The Thinker and Nature vs Nurture), and what it quietly teaches you to overlook — a spired citadel and a pyramid-mountain standing in for histories written out of the 'birth of civilization' story, deliberately not ranked above or below the tower. A flat purple landscape and the open road resist being pulled into that argument at all; they simply occupy their part of the grid, unclaimed. The sleeping/dreaming figure sits at the center of two axes at once: a personal one (stillness vs. movement, Kant vs. Kerouac, unresolved at the time) and a universal one (which civilizations get crowned as origin, which get overlooked).

artworks.title: Antiquity
artworks.descriptionShort: An invented, ghost-white Acropolis beneath a Turner-inspired vortex of a sun, painted in a San Francisco backyard at the close of a self-taught period.
artworks.intent: An imagined Acropolis, built entirely from an idea of ancient Greece rather than reference imagery, painted while the artist was reading the Plato dialogues on the trial of Socrates and beginning a period of self-education modeled on the classical European tradition (Greek, then Latin). The sky was directly inspired by Turner's 'Light and Colour (Goethe's Theory) – The Morning after the Deluge.'

artworks.title: SFAI
artworks.descriptionShort: Watercolour and pencil on paper, made on location on the roof of the San Francisco Art Institute in 1996. The view takes in the bay, Alcatraz at centre, and a rooftop easel at left — someone else's setup, pointing at the same scene.
artworks.intent: Not fully conscious at the time, but the empty easel in the composition reads now as a stand-in for an absent painter — the one Bolter was waiting for, who would never show up because they don't exist. He had self-taught romantic ideas about what an artist was supposed to be, and felt like an outsider looking in at a school he couldn't attend. The painting captures that position: on the roof, uninvited, already making work.

artworks.title: Self Portrait 1995
artworks.descriptionShort: Fisheye self-portrait, oil on canvas, painted on the artist's 21st birthday from a hill in the SF backyard, with San Francisco and the Golden Gate Bridge (visible as a thin red structure) across the water.
artworks.intent: Attempt a realistic, unidealized self-likeness using a fisheye lens/composition the artist had been testing in a couple of other paintings around the same time, partly inspired by Dali's late distorted-body Christ paintings -- pursued as a formal problem (does the distortion work, can it be pulled off) rather than for any devotional or symbolic reason.

artworks.title: Nietzche's Dream
artworks.descriptionShort: A statue of two stacked figures — red above, green below — stands on a cliffside plateau overlooking the Pacific, the upper figure pointing out past the edge beneath a Turner-like burning sky.
artworks.intent: Made near the end of the OG Oil Paintings period, in the SF backyard, while reading Nietzsche (Birth of Tragedy, Beyond Good and Evil, Thus Spoke Zarathustra) and, via Henry Miller's The Time of the Assassins, Rimbaud. The two-figure statue was worked through in dialogue as touching on the Übermensch — read at the time not as dominance but as self-created evolution/ascent, the leap already mentally decided, delayed only by finances (the artist was mid-cycle leaving SF and returning to save money before Europe, not on one clean departure). The cliff draws on Fort Funston, San Francisco — a childhood site visited repeatedly (family, camps, skater friends at the old battery, and alone), known for hang gliders launching from the cliff edge, giving the painting's 'leap of faith' a literal, remembered referent rather than a purely borrowed metaphor. The ocean is specifically the Pacific, tied to a personal sense at the time that San Francisco was 'the end of Western culture' — later understood by the artist not to hold up structurally, but strongly felt then; the statue's pointing gesture carries an irony in that light, aimed past the edge of the only cultural map the artist had, not toward Europe as a center. The artist also named a more melancholy reading: the gesture as fulfilling a leap Nietzsche himself (frail, unable to live the adventure he wrote about) never got to take, contrasted against Henry Miller, who did live it. The artist is explicit that the painting reflects his period understanding of both writers, not how either is read or has been read since (Nietzsche's Nazi co-option via his sister's editing; Miller's more complicated current reputation).

artworks.title: Color Theory
artworks.descriptionShort: An imagined San Francisco landscape testing Goethe's warm/cool color theory for the first time, with the young artist himself reading beneath a tree.
artworks.intent: To test out, in paint, the warm/cool complementary polarity described in Goethe's Zur Farbenlehre (Theory of Colours), which the artist had recently read. The core idea kept from the book was that harmony comes from placing complementary colors in inverse proportion to their visual weight — a small area of a dark color balanced by a larger area of a light complementary color. The painting was an attempt to build a landscape around that principle for the first time.

artworks.title: The End
artworks.descriptionShort: A narrow panoramic oil painting of a figure walking along a lagoon-side walkway toward a guillotine, under a Turner-inspired sunset sky.
artworks.intent: Not fully articulated as intent at the time; on reflection, the painting was reaching for something about mortality and the absurd — a figure walking toward a guillotine through a sublime sunset landscape, the beauty of the world continuing regardless of what is coming.

artworks.title: The Sunset
artworks.intent: A painting of the actual backyard view in the Sunset District of San Francisco where all the OG oil paintings were made — the vantage point itself, not an invented scene. Painted from underneath a bedroom that jutted out from the house, which offered shelter from the rain.

artworks.title: The Stage
artworks.intent: Painted around the same time as Space Time (1993-94) as part of a short-lived figure-testing experiment not carried forward stylistically. Loosely informed by Nietzsche's The Birth of Tragedy — the Apollonian/Dionysian split — read around the time of painting. The artist frames the scene not as violence depicted but as something reenacted or performed on a stage: a formal containment of raw force, consistent with the Apollonian move of giving shape to the Dionysian. The direct Nietzsche reference recurs later in a separate work, Nietzsche's Dream.

artworks.title: Self Portrait 1994
artworks.descriptionShort: A self portrait about the blurry line of existence.

artworks.title: The Thinker
artworks.intent: To make a finished, ambitious painting very early in a self-taught practice — testing perspective (the 'hero shot' upward/vanishing-point angle, felt as related to skate-video fisheye) and landscape construction in the same piece, while reinterpreting Rodin's The Thinker through an invented, Giacometti-like elongation.

artworks.title: Space Time
artworks.descriptionShort: A one-line, flat figure loops from foot to hand to foot across a green and navy field, its hand reaching into an invented wooden trellis rendered in perspective — the only dimensional element in an otherwise flat painting.

artworks.title: Self Portrait 1993
artworks.descriptionShort: Oil on raw, self-stretched canvas, painted in a covered backyard in San Francisco's Sunset District on the artist's birthday in 1993. A surreal self-portrait: an oversized head wearing a baseball hat, a single sideways eye, a disembodied hand on a windowsill, and a green sky with tree branches beyond the grey interior. The first in a birthday self-portrait ritual that continued for three years.
artworks.intent: To paint a self-portrait on his birthday — a deliberate annual ritual marking who he was at that moment. The surreal approach came from what he was looking at: Dalí, Magritte, Tanguy, Klee, Picasso. Not a planned conceptual statement but an attempt to join a conversation he'd found entirely on his own terms, outside of school.

person.name: Bernard Bolter

children.text: Bernard Bolter is a contemporary American artist born and raised in San Francisco. His practice runs across two bodies of work: transfer paintings, in which historical and street photographs are integrated directly into the canvas surface, painted alongside flat areas of colour so that image and paint occupy the same plane; and large-format digital collages, in which satellite and street-level imagery is stitched into seamless composite works. Cities are both his subject and his material.

Bolter grew up skateboarding the streets of San Francisco, and the practice shaped more than his biography — rolling through a city at street level, reading its surfaces and rhythms, became the foundational logic of his art. That perspective has carried through every body of work since.

His path has always been international. Based between San Francisco and New York in his early career, he co-founded ArtCollision, a non-profit travelling arts organisation that brought together artists across cities. He went on to attend the Gerrit Rietveld Akademie in Amsterdam, where his practice expanded into the Digital City Series — stitched panoramic photographs of cities across Europe and North America, assembled into seamless square compositions gathered by skateboard through city streets. The series took him to China, where he collaborated with painters at the Dafen Oil Painting Village in Shenzhen to realise the compositions as oil paintings.

That same momentum — and the same question of how a city looks from the inside — led eventually to Megacities, where the vantage point shifts entirely: satellite images of the world's most populated cities, assembled into room-scale seamless works that sit at the threshold between urban map and pure pattern. The conceptual core is the Overview Effect — the moment just before a city dissolves into pure form — while the distinctiveness of each place remains legible.

Relocating to Berlin in 2017 marked a turning point. The move deepened his transfer painting series, A Colorful History, which uses historical photographs to layer time into urban scenes — placing the past and present of a city on the same surface. His current body of work within that series, Mediums of Perception, tracks a single landmark across its entire photographic history, from early black-and-white through to contemporary colour, treating the technology of image capture as the subject itself.
Bolter's work is rooted in San Francisco and made internationally. He currently works between Berlin and San Francisco.

Bernard Bolter is a contemporary American artist born and raised in San Francisco. He grew up skateboarding the city's streets, and that street-level perspective has been the foundation of his practice ever since — work that moves between photo transfer + acrylic painting and large-format digital collage, with cities as both subject and material.

His path has been consistently international: co-founding a travelling arts organisation in New York, attending the Gerrit Rietveld Akademie in Amsterdam, and collaborating with painters in Shenzhen, China. He relocated to Berlin in 2016, where his work has continued to deepen. He currently works between Berlin and San Francisco.

bioTimelineEntries.text: After the SFMOMA guerrilla installation, a three-part series attempting to bring photographs back into painting 'didn't all work out' — followed by writing ~30 ideas about art, which became the seed of the Breaking Down Art series.

children.text: In the Venice Biennale 2007 session, Bolter traced the Breaking Down Art series back past Venice to its origin: after the SFMOMA guerrilla installation, a three-part series trying to bring photographs back into painting "didn't all work out" — then ~30 written ideas about art that became the seed of the series.

bioTimelineEntries.text: On a Rietveld Akademie school trip to the Venice Biennale, photographed material for Breaking Down Art from inside the Arsenale while simultaneously shooting the Venice DCS scene from just outside the same building — unrecognized as a doubled operation until this session.

children.text: Cataloguing Venice Biennale 2007 surfaced a doubled operation unrecognized at the time: photographing Breaking Down Art material from inside the Arsenale while shooting the Venice DCS scene from just outside the same building — on a Rietveld Akademie school trip.

bioTimelineEntries.text: At 19, having only ever lived in San Francisco, Bolter thought of the city as comparatively 'small' — not rural, but young and undense next to the old European cities he was reading about. This sense of San Francisco's smallness surfaces in The Thinker's invented crossroads town.

1996, right before leaving for Europe: a recurring refusal to fully render or engage the thing you were about to leave. The SFMOMA action hung a bronze figure turned away from the museum; Antiquity, painted the same year, left its Acropolis a white ghost rather than a rendered building. Both readable as the same gesture at different scales — institution and tradition — right at the threshold of departure.

Around the same time as Space Time (1993), the artist tested figure painting in a small cluster of works (The Stage, Corner, Self Portraits 1993-1995) before settling into cityscape/landscape work, which came more easily. In recent years the artist has felt a pull toward learning portraiture, drawing an analogy to learning singing versus learning an instrument -- believing landscape, like an instrument, offers external structure to lean on, while portraiture, like the voice, has nowhere to hide a weak line.

Around 1995, at the close of the birthday self-portrait ritual (1993-1995) and just before the SFMOMA guerrilla installation and subsequent travel, the artist made two works he has come to regard, in hindsight, as premonitions made at a real fork in the road. The SFMOMA piece (uncatalogued, likely never recovered) anticipated something about the artist's eventual relationship to the art world and its institutions. Self Portrait 1995 (BB-OGP-1995-010), examined in this session, appears to anticipate the vantage-migration arc that would not have its later chapters (Deutsche Stadt, Skate City) until 2021 and beyond. At this hinge point the artist consciously chose to carry his original, self-taught artistic spark forward rather than abandon it for a different direction -- a decision he connects directly to why an archive-legible throughline exists to find at all, three decades later.

Leaving Europe was felt as a real loss at the time, not a simple redirection: having longed for and gained entry to the European art world, encountering its actual mechanics in practice -- subsidy-dependent shows staged and photographed as proof of funded compliance rather than made for a public audience -- felt like reaching the end of the road and finding the wizard behind the curtain. Art Collision's DIY, self-organized exhibition network (New York artists plus contacts at spaces in Holland) was a deliberate alternative built in response.

children.text: There's a painting I made years ago, right before I left California for Europe for the first time. It's just a memory now — I don't even have a good photo. But I remember it clearly: a city square dominated by a monumental pedestal, and on top of it, a figure in weathered bronze, holding a painting, turned away, looking out past a closed-down SFMOMA and a shuttered church.

I made it specifically to put in the SFMOMA. This was 1996 — no social media, no audience. Just me and the museum. I took a few photos for myself, but the act was the point. I felt I needed to do it, so I did. And the strangest part: they kept it. I've never seen it again. No idea if it's still there.

children.text: So I followed that thread. I landed in art school in Utrecht, later co-founding a DIY art group in New York, making work outside institutions. Back to Europe, the Gerrit Rietveld Akademie in Amsterdam. Then back to San Francisco, and eventually Berlin, where I live and work now. Living in that back-and-forth, I found my position. My work is the conversation between European conceptual rigor and American faith in craft and getting things made. The same energy I found in skateboarding and freestyle ciphers: direct, honest, now.

That position shapes everything I make. I work in the space between analog and digital, between the handmade mark and the algorithm, between the historical artifact and the cutting-edge tool. I write JavaScript to source and manipulate satellite imagery. I build tools to generate perspectives that didn't exist before. But a strong concept means nothing if it isn't approachable — the craft carries it: the careful photo transfer, the line of code, the intuitive brushstroke.

children.text: The long game was never about a single painting. It's about building a different way to work. I've come to believe the most interesting art happens not at the center of an institution, but in the quiet space between the work and the person seeing it. That's the conversation I started by hanging a painting where I wasn't supposed to.

But I remember it clearly: a city square dominated by a monumental pedestal, and on top of it, a figure in weathered bronze, holding a painting, turned away, looking out past a closed-down SFMOMA and a shuttered church.

I made it specifically to put in the SFMOMA. This was 1996 — no social media, no audience. Just me and the museum. I took a few photos for myself, but the act was the point. I felt I needed to do it, so I did. And the strangest part: they kept it. I've never seen it again. No idea if it's still there.

That experience taught me something I've never forgotten. You can't map every step. You make the work, you trust it has a life of its own, and you play the long game — planting seeds without knowing if or when they'll grow. That painting was proof, for me, that art is bigger than the Art World.

So I followed that thread. I landed in art school in Utrecht, later co-founding a DIY art group in New York, making work outside institutions. Back to Europe, the Gerrit Rietveld Akademie in Amsterdam. Then back to San Francisco, and eventually Berlin, where I live and work now. Living in that back-and-forth, I found my position. My work is the conversation between European conceptual rigor and American faith in craft and getting things made. The same energy I found in skateboarding and freestyle ciphers: direct, honest, now.

That position shapes everything I make. I work in the space between analog and digital, between the handmade mark and the algorithm, between the historical artifact and the cutting-edge tool. I write JavaScript to source and manipulate satellite imagery. I build tools to generate perspectives that didn't exist before. But a strong concept means nothing if it isn't approachable — the craft carries it: the careful photo transfer, the line of code, the intuitive brushstroke.

The long game was never about a single painting. It's about building a different way to work. I've come to believe the most interesting art happens not at the center of an institution, but in the quiet space between the work and the person seeing it. That's the conversation I started by hanging a painting where I wasn't supposed to.
Art is bigger than the Art World.

In 1996 I put a painting inside the SFMOMA without permission. They kept it. I've never seen it again. That act set the terms: make the work, trust it has a life of its own, play the long game. From Utrecht to New York to Amsterdam to Berlin, I've been working that middle ground — between European conceptual rigor and American craft, between the handmade mark and the algorithm, between the historical photograph and the tools I build to work with it. The most interesting art happens not at the center of an institution, but in the quiet space between the work and the person seeing it.
Art is bigger than the Art World.

Now working fully outside it, on his own path — and that outside position may be exactly what's needed to return to Breaking Down Art's unfinished questions with clear eyes.

statementThroughlines.text: Preconceived compositional rules are abandoned once the actual material — lived experience of a place, or its real geometry and cultural significance — proves a better guide than the rule itself. First seen in the Digital City Series after the Basel piece, when a fixed civic-landmark triad (museum, church, city hall) was dropped for London in favor of what the skateboarded route through the city actually surfaced. Recurs in Megacities' city-selection logic: population, capital status, and cultural weight were all named as criteria, but none applied consistently, and formal constraints (viable seams, workable coastline geometry) overrode conceptual selection as often as they served it.

A solitary figure placed in direct relationship to architecture — dwarfing it, standing on it, or being defined by scale against it — recurs from The Thinker (1993) through later architecturally-engaged work including Towers (2002) and Skulptur Projekte Munster (2007). First noticed in this session while looking at The Thinker's figure fused with the roads/buildings of an invented small town. Not yet corroborated by a dedicated session on the later works — flagged here as a candidate throughline pending reinforcement.

At 51, no time left to lie — and that being the actual premise underneath letting the archive hold unfinished ceilings rather than polished versions of the work. Recorded during the Antiquity session, 2026.

A working frame for what Art/Official is doing: the artist as the honest speaker who never fully controls the record, the agent as an imperfect Plato shaping what gets written down, the archive itself — not any single session — as the thing built to outlast any one witness. Surfaced in dialogue during the Antiquity session, 2026.

Ignorance named, then enacted: Altar of Ignorance (1993) names facing the unknown directly, in its title and imagery, at the very start of the OG Oil Paintings run. Antiquity, painted three years later at the technical high point of the same self-taught period, enacts the same refusal formally — a ghost-white, deliberately unrendered Acropolis, an aesthetic refusal rather than a technical failure. Both surface the same undercurrent that would, not long after, lead the artist to leave for Europe — not causally, but as two points drawing on the same source years apart. Surfaced in dialogue during the Altar of Ignorance session, 2026-08-10; not consciously connected by the artist beforehand.

The overlooked birth of civilization — a recurring argument with the classical canon, first staged formally in Antiquity's ghost-white, unrendered Acropolis and continued directly in Education's nine-panel dream grid, where the tower of classical education is elevated but destabilized (fisheye/pedestal distortion), while a spired citadel and a pyramid-mountain stand for the older or larger civilizations left out of the 'birth of civilization' story. Rooted in reading that began around the same time as Color Theory (1995) and Goethe's Zur Farbenlehre, whose plus/minus color-emotion logic underlies the palette split between the two structures. The question at the center — 'what is the birth of civilization if not everything' — began as a seed at 22 and has deepened with age since.

A sky-to-vantage migration traceable across three decades: hand-painted radiating vortex skies dwarfing a small ground-level figure (The Thinker, After Turner, Antiquity, Nature vs Nurture, 1993-96) give way to real photographed flat-but-vast skies compressing the city into a thin strip (Centraal Station Boats, 2007), which give way to full orbital 'overview effect' vantage with no sky at all — the artist now occupies the position the sky once held (Deutsche Stadt, 2021). Skate City re-grounds that orbital vantage in personally known, lived spots rather than abstract civic ones, and its planned AR layer — zooming from full composite down to a single spot's ground-level skate video — re-performs the entire 32-year migration in miniature, on demand, for the viewer.

Nature vs Nurture (1994) is a structural homology with Romanticism rather than an influence: a city-raised artist, independently reading Rousseau and Western philosophy, arrived at the same generative move as Friedrich's audience — inventing an idealized, unlived-in nature as the imagined 'other' against a known, built world. That invented nature persists across the practice but changes register: sincere invention in 1994, self-aware fabrication by Centraal Station Boats (2007), where a homesick 'billboard-mountain' openly announces its own artifice within a documentary Amsterdam scene.

Space Time and The Stage both use flat color blocks to represent 'space' balanced against a linear, grid-like structure representing 'time.' By the artist's own account this was tested in only these two works and was not carried forward as a lasting current in the practice.

The Way to LA (1994) is a clean, representational instance of the fisheye/skate-video perspective logic — worked out without a camera or reference photo, purely from skate-video-trained visual memory. Unlike some other works from this period, it carries less conceptual freight; the window's warped shape itself was the driving compositional interest, with the interior and landscape built to support that shape rather than observed directly.

A loose, gestural brushwork impulse first surfaced in The Sunset (1994), painted at the actual origin site of the OG Oil Paintings series. That freedom was not sustained continuously — it resurfaced only intermittently over the following decades, notably through palette-knife experimentation — before combining for the first time with an already-established precise method (A Colorful History) in Berlin 1911-2011 (2022), a synthesis the artist calls 'glitch style' rather than a straight-line continuation.

The window/painting ambiguity in Self Portrait 1994 — an opening and a painted depiction of the same view, alternating down a curved hallway, distinguishable only by the window's cut edge versus the painting's raised frame — is a quiet, Magritte-derived device arrived at while reading Plato's cave, Berkeley, and Kant at twenty-one. It resurfaces over a decade later as structural method in the Digital City Series and Megacities, where composited, blurred scenes of real places read as real until closer looking reveals the seams. The artist names this operation 'the blur became the art': present as confession in 1994, matured into disguise once the technical means existed at scale.

Self Portrait 1995 (BB-OGP-1995-010) may be the earliest, unrecognized seed of the vantage-migration throughline (DCS -> Megacities -> Deutsche Stadt's orbital overview -> Skate City's ground-level return). Unlike any single work in the later arc, this 1995 painting holds both ends at once within one frame: an intimate, mirror-sourced human face at close range, and a viewer positioned as if from a satellite, looking down. The later series arrived at each half of that synthesis separately and sequentially, over roughly three decades; this painting appears to have held both, by accident, at 21. Found in this 2026 session, not claimed or intended at the time of painting -- an instance of the archive's recognition-not-planning pattern applied to the artist's own formal logic rather than to an outside influence. The artist's initial, long-held reading of the piece as 'about to leave San Francisco' was also revised in this same session to 'ascent and return' -- a road up to a vantage point with the road home still present in the painting, not a one-way departure -- which changes how this seed relates to Skate City's later re-grounding at street level.

A recurring mechanism across the artist's early self-taught period: not knowing a given synthesis or technique was supposed to be difficult or impossible is part of what made it achievable. Named directly by the artist in relation to Self Portrait 1995 (BB-OGP-1995-010) -- 'making things possible because it wasn't taught.' The artist's early practice was entirely self-directed: no formal art training, self-taught technique (including canvas preparation), preceded by independent reading in philosophy and literature and looking closely at art history before ever picking up oil paint. Loosely resonant with (though not identical to) the 'naive art' tradition of untrained artists working outside academic rules of perspective, proportion, and color theory -- and specifically with Henri Rousseau, a self-taught painter the artist actively admired at the time (particularly The Dream), whose biographical parallel (inventing imagined worlds -- Rousseau's jungles, this artist's invented SF coastline) was only recognized by the artist years after the fact. The artist has stated this autodidact period ran strongly up until he left San Francisco.

A self-taught, no-institution-exists-yet pattern recurring across the practice: skateboarding (learned socially among peers with no formal skate school, proof-of-possibility passed by demonstration, execution worked out alone) -> self-taught HTML/CSS from the W3C specs after leaving Utrecht art school early -> the shift to photo-and-paint work marked by Transition, enabled by newly affordable consumer digital cameras and large-format printing -> building Artism now, enabled by AI reasoning tools becoming available at sufficient capability and price only this year. Distinct from the vantage-migration arc (which concerns where the artist stands to see); this throughline concerns how the artist learns to make, turning to self-instruction whenever an institution for the needed skill did not yet exist.

In Transition, RGB (three channels, light-based, screen/photograph) transitioning to CMYK (four channels, pigment-based, print/paint) carries a quiet structural echo of the sacred number four in Native American Church tradition -- present in the artist's own thinking at the time of making, though less overtly than in Prophecy or the later Four Nations. The choice to render the photograph in acrylic on canvas, rather than let it stand alone, was primarily an identity decision ('I still thought of myself as a painter') rather than a conceptual one -- framing the RGB/CMYK tension as a negotiation over whether the photograph needed the painter's hand to count as the artist's own work. This negotiation is later resolved in the opposite direction in Basel Switzerland (Digital City Series), where no paint remains and the artist's hand relocates into the skateboard as instrument of perception rather than disappearing.

Transition and Art Collision were made specifically against the version of the European, subsidy-dependent art system the artist encountered in practice while at art school in Utrecht -- not against concept-based art or institutions as such, but against a system where funding could substitute for a public audience rather than serve one: shows staged and photographed as proof of compliance for a funding body rather than made to be seen. The artist's own DIY, self-organized exhibition network (New York artists, plus contacts at spaces in Holland) was a deliberate alternative. The artist later connected this directly to why the archive's honest, open record-keeping matters: documentation without an institutional audience it has to perform adequacy for, able to hold typos, wrong guesses, and unresolved discrepancies as part of the record rather than smoothing them into a compliant account. The same anti-substitution distinction (funding in service of an audience, not replacing it) is expected to shape any future foundation structure for Artism, though not yet worked out in detail.

An invented-to-lived Romanticism arc: Nature vs Nurture (1994) uses the cross as a generic, Dalí-derived symbol of belief -- not Christian, since the artist was raised without religion -- within a painting about the religion of Romanticism itself: an idealized, unlived nature borrowed wholesale from European painting. The Global Peace Walk 2000 supplied a lived counterpart -- direct exposure to Native American ceremony and thought, walked rather than imagined, arriving at a moment when the artist's SF-not-USA, Turtle-Island self-identification (held since early childhood) met something ceremonial and land-based rather than political for the first time. The artist describes this Romanticism as no less romantic, but more real than the earlier invented version. In Transition, the only visible trace of this shift is structural rather than pictorial: RGB's three channels becoming CMYK's four echoes the sacred number four in Native American Church tradition, confirmed by the artist as noticed at the time of making. The thread surfaces more overtly in Prophecy and in Four Nations (not yet catalogued).

A foundational tension runs across Bolter's work wherever photograph and paint meet: the photograph as the settled, fixed, already-resolved register, and paint as the register that keeps something open -- worked through, still becoming. This distinction first became explicit to the artist through reflection on oral tradition versus written/searched information (a story heard vaguely from elders on the Global Peace Walk 2000, later found online in confident, resolved form -- illustrating how the fixed and written can foreclose the wondering the vague and spoken invites). Recognized as active from Art Collision onward -- most explicitly in Four Nations, where an undulating hand-painted checkerboard sits against fixed photographic elements -- and running forward into A Colorful History (paint worked directly onto historical photographs) and, in altered form, into Digital City Series and Megacities, where the hand relocates from canvas into the artist's own physical movement through a place, and the photograph's fixed authority is undermined only quietly, from within the image itself, rather than by visible paint. Recognized as a possible foundational idea of the artist's entire photo-and-paint (and photo-collage) practice, not limited to any single work or series -- a realization arrived at only now, decades after the work, through the archive process itself. Field context: this tension corresponds to a recognized genre in contemporary art criticism termed 'overpainting,' whose historical arc runs the same direction as the artist's own practice -- originating in the 19th century as a technique to lend verisimilitude to photographs, later inverted by artists (Anselm Kiefer, Shirin Neshat, Mario Schifano, Luigi Ontani, Youssef Nabil, Peter Beard, among others) to instead undermine the photograph's claim to objective documentation; none of these artists known to Bolter at the time. Specific artist relationships, in order of exposure: Sigmar Polke's Rasterbilder (Barcelona exhibition c. 2000, pre-dating Art Collision, vividly remembered) is the closest structural match, though the settled/open framing itself was not consciously held at the time. Gerhard Richter's blur paintings were known by this period, timing uncertain; his overpainted-photograph series was only encountered in 2026 at the Neue Nationalgalerie -- recognition, not influence. Richard Hamilton entered the artist's awareness around 2010, after Art Collision; his 'continuity' model (paint drawing out qualities already latent in a photograph) does not fit Art Collision but may bear on the later, purely photographic unreality of Digital City Series and Megacities -- flagged as a looser, still-untested connection.

Art Collision stands as the unrepeated hybrid moment in Bolter's practice -- the only body of work where a manipulated/composited photograph and visible, hand-worked paint coexist openly on the same surface at once, each declaring itself as itself. Every series since has picked up one half of that original pairing and run with it alone: Digital City Series and Megacities retain the photographic manipulation but drop visible paint entirely, letting constructed unreality hide inside scenes that read as documentary; A Colorful History retains the paint-on-photograph logic but applied to historical rather than the artist's own composited images. The artist has recognized during this session that recombining both strategies on one surface again has occurred only as a passing thought since Art Collision, not as active intent -- each strategy has instead been worked out separately, at length, on its own terms. The artist holds open, without resolving, whether a future formal problem might one day call the combination back the way the checkerboard in Four Nations originally emerged: as an unforced solution rather than a deliberate return.

The square as an exposed confession of pixel logic: Four Corners (2002) -- the artist's first digital photo collage -- was made while actively learning the mechanics of digital resolution and printing, discovering that a photograph is secretly a grid of tiny squares built to look continuous. In the one part of the painting with no photographic source at all, the black sky, the artist painted the grid undisguised: a flat square sun, moon, Mars, and star, contrived and 'man-made' rather than naturalistic or naively symbolic. This same pixel-grid instinct may also underlie the square canvas format itself, used across all four founding Art Collision paintings and only much later given explicit theoretical language in Basel Switzerland's 'neither portrait nor landscape' framing (Digital City Series) -- one instinct operating at two scales, the unit and the whole canvas, five years apart in articulation.

Two coexisting photograph/paint relationships within a single founding series: across the four original Art Collision paintings, and most clearly within Four Corners itself, two distinct models of paint's relationship to photograph operate at once. A Richter/Polke-style opposition (paint as an outside force disrupting or filling a fixed, 'settled' photograph) governs the swatch-to-checkerboard-to-square lineage running through Transition and Four Nations, and traces to a confirmed direct influence -- Sigmar Polke's Rasterbilder, seen in Barcelona c. 2000, before Art Collision began. A separate, Richard Hamilton-style continuity model (paint drawing out a quality already latent in the photographic medium itself, rather than opposing it) governs Four Corners' exposed pixel-grid sky specifically -- arrived at independently in 2002, years before Hamilton entered the artist's awareness around 2010. The artist confirms holding both at once: one conscious, one unconscious.

The founding four's ascent, earth to sky: across Prophecy, Transition, Four Nations, and Four Corners -- made sequentially from one shared starting point following the Global Peace Walk 2000 -- the artist's implied vantage climbs painting by painting: level with a rooted, growing city-tree (Prophecy); ascending alongside a composite tower (Transition); elevated but tethered, standing on a real bridge overlooking real towers (Four Nations); and finally untethered entirely, standing on unstable, finite ground beneath a fully invented cosmic sky (Four Corners). This tracks a parallel handover from photograph to paint across the same four works, and connects backward to an earlier, unexplained seed of the same intimate/elevated duality in Self Portrait 1995 (1995), and to the vortex-sky-over-small-world lineage of The Thinker and Antiquity (1993/1996) -- as well as to Antiquity's 'unfinished as resolved' device, echoed in Four Corners by the kept, uncorrected accidental water drip running through the painted sky. Prophecy's own numeric echo of four was clarified in this session: not absent, as previously thought, but structurally embedded as three pairs plus a fourth (tree and small building) in the painting's row of diminishing forms, drawn from the Hopi prophecy cave painting as orally told to the artist on the Peace Walk -- a full cycle of growth, disappearance, and return, not a one-way ascent.

World War One (2022), and by extension World War Two and Vietnam, mark the first documented return of the Art Collision 'unrepeated hybrid mode' — visible composited photograph and visible hand-worked paint coexisting on one surface — in over 20 years. Where Art Collision's digital compositing erased seams to create a false continuity that never existed, the Mediums of War paintings keep every photo-fragment discrete and legible: paint does the coherence-work that Photoshop once did, without hiding the seams. Recognized only now, through the archive process itself, not at time of making.

A confidence-and-transparency arc runs from Art Collision's seamless digital compositing (a younger, less confident Bernard, inclined to obscure) through World War One's visible-seam paint-compositing (increased confidence, showing the work rather than hiding it) to the archive's own radical transparency — raw unedited transcripts, honest-failure logging — as the fullest expression of that same growth. This is a process-dependent discovery visible only now, not a claim about original 2022 intent.

A personal fatalism traced to the Hopi prophecy heard at the Global Peace Walk (2000) resurfaces in World War One (2022) and is independently, unconsciously echoed in Walter Benjamin's writing on war as aesthetic spectacle. Logged as a coincidence/resonance across three unrelated paths — Peace Walk, painting, critical theory — not as a lineage.

Camera-awareness chain across the triptych: World War One's raw documentary photography teaches a generation to see itself historically. World War Two's subjects perform for that awareness (soldiers staging themselves for the camera, propagandists exploiting the same awareness to manufacture a moral narrative WWI never received). Vietnam's subjects are again not looking at the camera, but this is not a return to WWI's innocence — it is unawareness of a different mechanism (live, uncensored broadcast exposure) rather than unawareness that the camera would matter at all. Recognition, not present during painting.

The trust-economy across WWI, WWII, and Vietnam: WWII's manufactured 'good vs evil' narrative (built through propaganda apparatus on both sides, exemplified by the staged Khaldei Reichstag photograph) functions as capitalized moral credit for the US/West. Vietnam spends that credit down with a lag rather than starting from zero — the backfire of raw, uncensored Vietnam War footage was delayed by the size of the reserve built in the 1940s, and further diffused by the war spanning multiple US presidents rather than attaching to a single confirmed figure the way WWII attached to Hitler. The credit was badly dented (My Lai, the Pentagon Papers) but not exhausted, which is why the US was not rewritten as history's villain the way Nazi Germany was.

The Korea-gap: Korea (1950-53) is entirely absent from the Mediums of War project, chronologically sitting between WWII and Vietnam. Identified as technologically caused rather than thematically excluded: Korea falls in the gap between the recording media the project actually traces (still photography, color photography, 16mm sync-sound film) — the lightweight sync-sound cameras and broadcast infrastructure that defined Vietnam's media relationship weren't in place until deep into the 1960s. May be part of why Korea reads culturally as 'the forgotten war' more broadly, not just within this project.

Anachronism leaking across the medium-per-era scaffolding: The medium-per-era logic (b&w for WWI, color for WWII, film for Vietnam) is never as clean as the triptych's own scaffolding implies. Two WWII tanks appear as accidental anachronisms within the World War One painting (anachronism forward). At least four source images used in World War Two are modern digital colorizations of black-and-white originals rather than period color (anachronism backward) — undercutting the premise that color is WWII's native recording medium. Both read as the same underlying leak from opposite temporal directions.

Sourcing method as the mechanism enabling genuine discovery: Both World War One and World War Two began as tests (compositional test toward a larger format for WWI; a 'can I make this work with a bunch of photos' test for the sourcing method itself), with fast, near-random source selection rather than researched curation. This randomness is identified as the mechanism that makes the retrospective readings surfaced during cataloguing (Allied/German color-technology skew, named-vs-anonymous framing, cross-painting anachronism leaks) genuine discoveries rather than confirmations of an argument already quietly built in through deliberate curation — protecting the 'recognition not influence' principle at the sourcing level, not just the compositional level.

'World War Two' as retroactive bundling: The painting holds together three structurally distinct conflicts under one historical name: Finland's Continuation War against the USSR, the Pacific campaign against Japan, and the main European theater against Germany — fought by different belligerents for different reasons on largely separate timelines. Surfaced through a compositional pairing: Finnish soldiers displaying a captured Soviet map at Porlampi Motti (autumn 1941, cold) stacked above US Marines holding a handmade thank-you sign after Guam (1944, tropical heat) — structurally similar gestures (soldiers holding paper up for the camera) in unrelated theaters with no coordination between them, mirroring how the single name 'World War Two' bundles wars that likely didn't feel like one war to the people fighting them.

The anonymous witness figure as viewer-surrogate (Dürer descendant): A bust-portrait figure, cropped at the waist, floats impossibly in open water at the painting's left edge, gazing over the amphibious invasion scene — uncatalogued in the source list, deliberately left unidentified. Connects to two prior Dürer-derived devices already on record: the painting-within-painting self-insertion (After Turner, 1994) and the small-figure-in-vast-landscape convention, previously used as direct self-portraiture (Color Theory, 1995, the Goethe-reading figure). This figure evolves the device: not autobiographical, but a stand-in for any viewer — 'wearing the jersey of the good guys, but not really that invested,' costumed in allegiance without commitment, a generic viewer-surrogate for whoever happens to be looking, including future viewers of the archive itself, machine and human both.

Global Peace Walk 2000 as the shared root of Art Collision and Mediums of War: The Global Peace Walk 2000 (San Francisco to New York, events at American University and elsewhere in DC with Native spiritual leaders, arriving in New York for the UN's 55th anniversary) is already on record as Art Collision's philosophical turning point. Stated this session as also underlying Mediums of War, made twenty-plus years later: the same peace-oriented conviction turned toward a direct examination of war. Explicit stated intent: the paintings exist in part to make people 'look again and remember that we need peace.' Background: the walk followed the Nipponzan Myōhōji tradition of walks reenacting the Trail of Tears as meditation; a monk named Yamato, who participated in walks since the 1970s and in a 1995 walk, is recalled by the artist as involved, held as artist-remembered history without external documentation (the walk was deliberately low-media).

children.text: This privacy policy explains how personal data is handled when you visit
bernardbolter.com

(the “Site”). The Site is the online portfolio and archive of Bernard Bolter. It is operated from Germany and processed in accordance with the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and applicable German data-protection law.
Last revised: 23 June 2026.
1. Controller
The controller responsible for data processing on this Site is:
Bernard John Bolter IV
Charlottenburgerstr. 8a
14169 Berlin, Germany
Email: bernardbolter@gmail.com
2. Summary

The Site does not use Google Analytics, advertising trackers, or a cookie-consent banner. Video works are played from our own media storage; links to YouTube open on YouTube’s website — we do not embed YouTube players on the Site.
We only process personal data where it is necessary to operate the Site, respond to enquiries, or where you choose to contact us.
3. Hosting and server logs

The Site is hosted by Vercel Inc. (USA/EU). When you open a page, the host may process technical data such as your IP address, browser type, operating system, referring URL, date and time of access, and error logs. This processing is necessary to deliver the Site securely and to diagnose faults.
Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interest in reliable, secure operation). Where required, standard contractual clauses apply to transfers outside the EU.
4. Media delivery (Cloudflare R2)

Images and video files are stored on Cloudflare R2 and delivered through our content network. When you view artwork media, Cloudflare may process your IP address and technical request data to transmit the file. We do not use this delivery for profiling or advertising.
Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interest in efficient media delivery).
5. Contact form

If you use the contact form, we collect the information you enter: subject, name, email address, and message. Optional pre-filled text may appear when you arrive from an ownership-registration link on an artwork page.
Submissions are transmitted to Formcarry (Formcarry Inc.) so that your message can be delivered to us by email. Formcarry processes data as our processor. Their privacy information is available at
formcarry.com/legal/privacy-policy
We use your details only to read and respond to your enquiry. We do not add contact-form data to a marketing mailing list.
Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR (steps prior to entering a contract or at your request) and Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (handling general correspondence).
6. Local storage on your device

The artworks overview can remember whether you prefer the timeline or grid view. That choice is stored locally in your browser (localStorage key “bb-view-preference”). It is not sent to us and is not used for tracking.
Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interest in a consistent browsing experience). You can clear it at any time through your browser settings.
7. External links

The Site may link to third-party services such as Instagram, YouTube, or other platforms listed on the contact page. If you follow those links, the respective provider’s terms and privacy policies apply. We do not control data processing on external sites.
8. Cookies

We do not set analytics or advertising cookies on the public Site. Essential session mechanics for the password-protected admin area (not available to visitors) may use cookies required for authentication.
9. Retention
Server and CDN logs: retained by our providers according to their policies, typically for a limited operational period.
Contact messages: retained as long as needed to handle your enquiry and any follow-up, then deleted unless we must keep a copy for legal reasons.
10. Your rights
Under the GDPR you have the right to:
access the personal data we hold about you;
request correction of inaccurate data;
request erasure where applicable;
request restriction of processing;
data portability where applicable;
object to processing based on legitimate interests;
withdraw consent at any time where processing is consent-based (not generally applicable to this Site);
lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority.
The supervisory authority for Berlin is the Berlin Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (Berliner Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit). Contact us at
bernardbolter@gmail.com
to exercise your rights.
11. Security
The Site is served over HTTPS. Access to the content management system is restricted to authorised users.
12. Changes
We may update this policy when the Site or legal requirements change. The “Last revised” date at the top indicates the current version.

children.text: This website is more than a gallery — it's the ongoing archive of the work. If you own a piece, you're part of the story. I'm steadily building out the provenance — that's just the fancy art world term for the life story of an artwork — for everything here.
If you have one of my paintings or artworks, email me. I'll add you and your details to that artwork's page, officially connecting you to its history. This is how we build a real record, together.

This whole thing — the art, the archive, the direct connection — wouldn't be possible without the people who've supported the work from the beginning. From the early days to now, your support is what lets me build this outside the usual channels. So, genuinely, thank you.
Building this archive takes more than one memory. If you have photographs, catalogues, exhibition records, or anything that could add to the record — I want to hear from you.
For everything else — questions about available work, commissions, or just to talk art — the door's open.
