bioEntries.text: After the SFMOMA guerrilla installation, a three-part series attempting to bring photographs back into painting 'didn't all work out' — followed by writing ~30 ideas about art, which became the seed of the Breaking Down Art series.

On a Rietveld Akademie school trip to the Venice Biennale, photographed material for Breaking Down Art from inside the Arsenale while simultaneously shooting the Venice DCS scene from just outside the same building — unrecognized as a doubled operation until this session.

At 19, having only ever lived in San Francisco, Bolter thought of the city as comparatively 'small' — not rural, but young and undense next to the old European cities he was reading about. This sense of San Francisco's smallness surfaces in The Thinker's invented crossroads town.

1996, right before leaving for Europe: a recurring refusal to fully render or engage the thing you were about to leave. The SFMOMA action hung a bronze figure turned away from the museum; Antiquity, painted the same year, left its Acropolis a white ghost rather than a rendered building. Both readable as the same gesture at different scales — institution and tradition — right at the threshold of departure.

Around the same time as Space Time (1993), the artist tested figure painting in a small cluster of works (The Stage, Corner, Self Portraits 1993-1995) before settling into cityscape/landscape work, which came more easily. In recent years the artist has felt a pull toward learning portraiture, drawing an analogy to learning singing versus learning an instrument -- believing landscape, like an instrument, offers external structure to lean on, while portraiture, like the voice, has nowhere to hide a weak line.

Around 1995, at the close of the birthday self-portrait ritual (1993-1995) and just before the SFMOMA guerrilla installation and subsequent travel, the artist made two works he has come to regard, in hindsight, as premonitions made at a real fork in the road. The SFMOMA piece (uncatalogued, likely never recovered) anticipated something about the artist's eventual relationship to the art world and its institutions. Self Portrait 1995 (BB-OGP-1995-010), examined in this session, appears to anticipate the vantage-migration arc that would not have its later chapters (Deutsche Stadt, Skate City) until 2021 and beyond. At this hinge point the artist consciously chose to carry his original, self-taught artistic spark forward rather than abandon it for a different direction -- a decision he connects directly to why an archive-legible throughline exists to find at all, three decades later.

Left Hoge School voor de Kunsten (Utrecht) before completing the program after finding the teaching inadequate; began self-teaching HTML and CSS directly from the W3C specifications during the same period. Worked briefly as a junior art director at a web company before the dot-com bubble burst, then joined the Global Peace Walk 2000 partway through its east coast leg, walking with the group into New York and settling there afterward -- the period from which Transition and the first Art Collision works emerge.

Left Hoge School voor de Kunsten (Utrecht) before completing the program: the concept-based curriculum was a shock, and in practice felt like cover for the teachers not teaching technique. Began self-teaching HTML and CSS directly from the W3C specifications during the same period. Worked briefly as a junior art director at a web company before the dot-com bubble burst, then joined the Global Peace Walk 2000 partway through its east coast leg, walking with the group into New York and settling there afterward -- the period from which Transition and the first Art Collision works emerge. Leaving Europe was felt as a real loss at the time, not a simple redirection: having longed for and gained entry to the European art world, encountering its actual mechanics in practice -- subsidy-dependent shows staged and photographed as proof of funded compliance rather than made for a public audience -- felt like reaching the end of the road and finding the wizard behind the curtain. Art Collision's DIY, self-organized exhibition network (New York artists plus contacts at spaces in Holland) was a deliberate alternative built in response.

throughlines.text: A recurring inside/outside position: in 2007–08, working from inside the art school system, half in awe of a world he wasn't sure he belonged to. Now working fully outside it, on his own path — and that outside position may be exactly what's needed to return to Breaking Down Art's unfinished questions with clear eyes.

Preconceived compositional rules are abandoned once the actual material — lived experience of a place, or its real geometry and cultural significance — proves a better guide than the rule itself. First seen in the Digital City Series after the Basel piece, when a fixed civic-landmark triad (museum, church, city hall) was dropped for London in favor of what the skateboarded route through the city actually surfaced. Recurs in Megacities' city-selection logic: population, capital status, and cultural weight were all named as criteria, but none applied consistently, and formal constraints (viable seams, workable coastline geometry) overrode conceptual selection as often as they served it.

A solitary figure placed in direct relationship to architecture — dwarfing it, standing on it, or being defined by scale against it — recurs from The Thinker (1993) through later architecturally-engaged work including Towers (2002) and Skulptur Projekte Munster (2007). First noticed in this session while looking at The Thinker's figure fused with the roads/buildings of an invented small town. Not yet corroborated by a dedicated session on the later works — flagged here as a candidate throughline pending reinforcement.

At 51, no time left to lie — and that being the actual premise underneath letting the archive hold unfinished ceilings rather than polished versions of the work. Recorded during the Antiquity session, 2026.

A working frame for what Art/Official is doing: the artist as the honest speaker who never fully controls the record, the agent as an imperfect Plato shaping what gets written down, the archive itself — not any single session — as the thing built to outlast any one witness. Surfaced in dialogue during the Antiquity session, 2026.

Ignorance named, then enacted: Altar of Ignorance (1993) names facing the unknown directly, in its title and imagery, at the very start of the OG Oil Paintings run. Antiquity, painted three years later at the technical high point of the same self-taught period, enacts the same refusal formally — a ghost-white, deliberately unrendered Acropolis, an aesthetic refusal rather than a technical failure. Both surface the same undercurrent that would, not long after, lead the artist to leave for Europe — not causally, but as two points drawing on the same source years apart. Surfaced in dialogue during the Altar of Ignorance session, 2026-08-10; not consciously connected by the artist beforehand.

The overlooked birth of civilization — a recurring argument with the classical canon, first staged formally in Antiquity's ghost-white, unrendered Acropolis and continued directly in Education's nine-panel dream grid, where the tower of classical education is elevated but destabilized (fisheye/pedestal distortion), while a spired citadel and a pyramid-mountain stand for the older or larger civilizations left out of the 'birth of civilization' story. Rooted in reading that began around the same time as Color Theory (1995) and Goethe's Zur Farbenlehre, whose plus/minus color-emotion logic underlies the palette split between the two structures. The question at the center — 'what is the birth of civilization if not everything' — began as a seed at 22 and has deepened with age since.

A sky-to-vantage migration traceable across three decades: hand-painted radiating vortex skies dwarfing a small ground-level figure (The Thinker, After Turner, Antiquity, Nature vs Nurture, 1993-96) give way to real photographed flat-but-vast skies compressing the city into a thin strip (Centraal Station Boats, 2007), which give way to full orbital 'overview effect' vantage with no sky at all — the artist now occupies the position the sky once held (Deutsche Stadt, 2021). Skate City re-grounds that orbital vantage in personally known, lived spots rather than abstract civic ones, and its planned AR layer — zooming from full composite down to a single spot's ground-level skate video — re-performs the entire 32-year migration in miniature, on demand, for the viewer.

Nature vs Nurture (1994) is a structural homology with Romanticism rather than an influence: a city-raised artist, independently reading Rousseau and Western philosophy, arrived at the same generative move as Friedrich's audience — inventing an idealized, unlived-in nature as the imagined 'other' against a known, built world. That invented nature persists across the practice but changes register: sincere invention in 1994, self-aware fabrication by Centraal Station Boats (2007), where a homesick 'billboard-mountain' openly announces its own artifice within a documentary Amsterdam scene.

Space Time and The Stage both use flat color blocks to represent 'space' balanced against a linear, grid-like structure representing 'time.' By the artist's own account this was tested in only these two works and was not carried forward as a lasting current in the practice.

The Way to LA (1994) is a clean, representational instance of the fisheye/skate-video perspective logic — worked out without a camera or reference photo, purely from skate-video-trained visual memory. Unlike some other works from this period, it carries less conceptual freight; the window's warped shape itself was the driving compositional interest, with the interior and landscape built to support that shape rather than observed directly.

A loose, gestural brushwork impulse first surfaced in The Sunset (1994), painted at the actual origin site of the OG Oil Paintings series. That freedom was not sustained continuously — it resurfaced only intermittently over the following decades, notably through palette-knife experimentation — before combining for the first time with an already-established precise method (A Colorful History) in Berlin 1911-2011 (2022), a synthesis the artist calls 'glitch style' rather than a straight-line continuation.

The window/painting ambiguity in Self Portrait 1994 — an opening and a painted depiction of the same view, alternating down a curved hallway, distinguishable only by the window's cut edge versus the painting's raised frame — is a quiet, Magritte-derived device arrived at while reading Plato's cave, Berkeley, and Kant at twenty-one. It resurfaces over a decade later as structural method in the Digital City Series and Megacities, where composited, blurred scenes of real places read as real until closer looking reveals the seams. The artist names this operation 'the blur became the art': present as confession in 1994, matured into disguise once the technical means existed at scale.

Self Portrait 1995 (BB-OGP-1995-010) may be the earliest, unrecognized seed of the vantage-migration throughline (DCS -> Megacities -> Deutsche Stadt's orbital overview -> Skate City's ground-level return). Unlike any single work in the later arc, this 1995 painting holds both ends at once within one frame: an intimate, mirror-sourced human face at close range, and a viewer positioned as if from a satellite, looking down. The later series arrived at each half of that synthesis separately and sequentially, over roughly three decades; this painting appears to have held both, by accident, at 21. Found in this 2026 session, not claimed or intended at the time of painting -- an instance of the archive's recognition-not-planning pattern applied to the artist's own formal logic rather than to an outside influence. The artist's initial, long-held reading of the piece as 'about to leave San Francisco' was also revised in this same session to 'ascent and return' -- a road up to a vantage point with the road home still present in the painting, not a one-way departure -- which changes how this seed relates to Skate City's later re-grounding at street level.

A recurring mechanism across the artist's early self-taught period: not knowing a given synthesis or technique was supposed to be difficult or impossible is part of what made it achievable. Named directly by the artist in relation to Self Portrait 1995 (BB-OGP-1995-010) -- 'making things possible because it wasn't taught.' The artist's early practice was entirely self-directed: no formal art training, self-taught technique (including canvas preparation), preceded by independent reading in philosophy and literature and looking closely at art history before ever picking up oil paint. Loosely resonant with (though not identical to) the 'naive art' tradition of untrained artists working outside academic rules of perspective, proportion, and color theory -- and specifically with Henri Rousseau, a self-taught painter the artist actively admired at the time (particularly The Dream), whose biographical parallel (inventing imagined worlds -- Rousseau's jungles, this artist's invented SF coastline) was only recognized by the artist years after the fact. The artist has stated this autodidact period ran strongly up until he left San Francisco.

A self-taught, no-institution-exists-yet pattern recurring across the practice: skateboarding (learned socially among peers with no formal skate school, proof-of-possibility passed by demonstration, execution worked out alone) -> self-taught HTML/CSS from the W3C specs after leaving Utrecht art school early -> the shift to photo-and-paint work marked by Transition, enabled by newly affordable consumer digital cameras and large-format printing -> building Artism now, enabled by AI reasoning tools becoming available at sufficient capability and price only this year. Distinct from the vantage-migration arc (which concerns where the artist stands to see); this throughline concerns how the artist learns to make, turning to self-instruction whenever an institution for the needed skill did not yet exist.

In Transition, RGB (three channels, light-based, screen/photograph) transitioning to CMYK (four channels, pigment-based, print/paint) carries a quiet structural echo of the sacred number four in Native American Church tradition -- present in the artist's own thinking at the time of making, though less overtly than in Prophecy or the later Four Nations. The choice to render the photograph in acrylic on canvas, rather than let it stand alone, was primarily an identity decision ('I still thought of myself as a painter') rather than a conceptual one -- framing the RGB/CMYK tension as a negotiation over whether the photograph needed the painter's hand to count as the artist's own work. This negotiation is later resolved in the opposite direction in Basel Switzerland (Digital City Series), where no paint remains and the artist's hand relocates into the skateboard as instrument of perception rather than disappearing.

Transition and Art Collision were made specifically against the version of the European, subsidy-dependent art system the artist encountered in practice while at art school in Utrecht -- not against concept-based art or institutions as such, but against a system where funding could substitute for a public audience rather than serve one: shows staged and photographed as proof of compliance for a funding body rather than made to be seen. The artist's own DIY, self-organized exhibition network (New York artists, plus contacts at spaces in Holland) was a deliberate alternative. The artist later connected this directly to why the archive's honest, open record-keeping matters: documentation without an institutional audience it has to perform adequacy for, able to hold typos, wrong guesses, and unresolved discrepancies as part of the record rather than smoothing them into a compliant account. The same anti-substitution distinction (funding in service of an audience, not replacing it) is expected to shape any future foundation structure for Artism, though not yet worked out in detail.

An invented-to-lived Romanticism arc: Nature vs Nurture (1994) uses the cross as a generic, Dalí-derived symbol of belief -- not Christian, since the artist was raised without religion -- within a painting about the religion of Romanticism itself: an idealized, unlived nature borrowed wholesale from European painting. The Global Peace Walk 2000 supplied a lived counterpart -- direct exposure to Native American ceremony and thought, walked rather than imagined, arriving at a moment when the artist's SF-not-USA, Turtle-Island self-identification (held since early childhood) met something ceremonial and land-based rather than political for the first time. The artist describes this Romanticism as no less romantic, but more real than the earlier invented version. In Transition, the only visible trace of this shift is structural rather than pictorial: RGB's three channels becoming CMYK's four echoes the sacred number four in Native American Church tradition, confirmed by the artist as noticed at the time of making. The thread surfaces more overtly in Prophecy and in Four Nations (not yet catalogued).

A foundational tension runs across Bolter's work wherever photograph and paint meet: the photograph as the settled, fixed, already-resolved register, and paint as the register that keeps something open -- worked through, still becoming. This distinction first became explicit to the artist through reflection on oral tradition versus written/searched information (a story heard vaguely from elders on the Global Peace Walk 2000, later found online in confident, resolved form -- illustrating how the fixed and written can foreclose the wondering the vague and spoken invites). Recognized as active from Art Collision onward -- most explicitly in Four Nations, where an undulating hand-painted checkerboard sits against fixed photographic elements -- and running forward into A Colorful History (paint worked directly onto historical photographs) and, in altered form, into Digital City Series and Megacities, where the hand relocates from canvas into the artist's own physical movement through a place, and the photograph's fixed authority is undermined only quietly, from within the image itself, rather than by visible paint. Recognized as a possible foundational idea of the artist's entire photo-and-paint (and photo-collage) practice, not limited to any single work or series -- a realization arrived at only now, decades after the work, through the archive process itself. Field context: this tension corresponds to a recognized genre in contemporary art criticism termed 'overpainting,' whose historical arc runs the same direction as the artist's own practice -- originating in the 19th century as a technique to lend verisimilitude to photographs, later inverted by artists (Anselm Kiefer, Shirin Neshat, Mario Schifano, Luigi Ontani, Youssef Nabil, Peter Beard, among others) to instead undermine the photograph's claim to objective documentation; none of these artists known to Bolter at the time. Specific artist relationships, in order of exposure: Sigmar Polke's Rasterbilder (Barcelona exhibition c. 2000, pre-dating Art Collision, vividly remembered) is the closest structural match, though the settled/open framing itself was not consciously held at the time. Gerhard Richter's blur paintings were known by this period, timing uncertain; his overpainted-photograph series was only encountered in 2026 at the Neue Nationalgalerie -- recognition, not influence. Richard Hamilton entered the artist's awareness around 2010, after Art Collision; his 'continuity' model (paint drawing out qualities already latent in a photograph) does not fit Art Collision but may bear on the later, purely photographic unreality of Digital City Series and Megacities -- flagged as a looser, still-untested connection.

Art Collision stands as the unrepeated hybrid moment in Bolter's practice -- the only body of work where a manipulated/composited photograph and visible, hand-worked paint coexist openly on the same surface at once, each declaring itself as itself. Every series since has picked up one half of that original pairing and run with it alone: Digital City Series and Megacities retain the photographic manipulation but drop visible paint entirely, letting constructed unreality hide inside scenes that read as documentary; A Colorful History retains the paint-on-photograph logic but applied to historical rather than the artist's own composited images. The artist has recognized during this session that recombining both strategies on one surface again has occurred only as a passing thought since Art Collision, not as active intent -- each strategy has instead been worked out separately, at length, on its own terms. The artist holds open, without resolving, whether a future formal problem might one day call the combination back the way the checkerboard in Four Nations originally emerged: as an unforced solution rather than a deliberate return.

The square as an exposed confession of pixel logic: Four Corners (2002) -- the artist's first digital photo collage -- was made while actively learning the mechanics of digital resolution and printing, discovering that a photograph is secretly a grid of tiny squares built to look continuous. In the one part of the painting with no photographic source at all, the black sky, the artist painted the grid undisguised: a flat square sun, moon, Mars, and star, contrived and 'man-made' rather than naturalistic or naively symbolic. This same pixel-grid instinct may also underlie the square canvas format itself, used across all four founding Art Collision paintings and only much later given explicit theoretical language in Basel Switzerland's 'neither portrait nor landscape' framing (Digital City Series) -- one instinct operating at two scales, the unit and the whole canvas, five years apart in articulation.

Two coexisting photograph/paint relationships within a single founding series: across the four original Art Collision paintings, and most clearly within Four Corners itself, two distinct models of paint's relationship to photograph operate at once. A Richter/Polke-style opposition (paint as an outside force disrupting or filling a fixed, 'settled' photograph) governs the swatch-to-checkerboard-to-square lineage running through Transition and Four Nations, and traces to a confirmed direct influence -- Sigmar Polke's Rasterbilder, seen in Barcelona c. 2000, before Art Collision began. A separate, Richard Hamilton-style continuity model (paint drawing out a quality already latent in the photographic medium itself, rather than opposing it) governs Four Corners' exposed pixel-grid sky specifically -- arrived at independently in 2002, years before Hamilton entered the artist's awareness around 2010. The artist confirms holding both at once: one conscious, one unconscious.

The founding four's ascent, earth to sky: across Prophecy, Transition, Four Nations, and Four Corners -- made sequentially from one shared starting point following the Global Peace Walk 2000 -- the artist's implied vantage climbs painting by painting: level with a rooted, growing city-tree (Prophecy); ascending alongside a composite tower (Transition); elevated but tethered, standing on a real bridge overlooking real towers (Four Nations); and finally untethered entirely, standing on unstable, finite ground beneath a fully invented cosmic sky (Four Corners). This tracks a parallel handover from photograph to paint across the same four works, and connects backward to an earlier, unexplained seed of the same intimate/elevated duality in Self Portrait 1995 (1995), and to the vortex-sky-over-small-world lineage of The Thinker and Antiquity (1993/1996) -- as well as to Antiquity's 'unfinished as resolved' device, echoed in Four Corners by the kept, uncorrected accidental water drip running through the painted sky. Prophecy's own numeric echo of four was clarified in this session: not absent, as previously thought, but structurally embedded as three pairs plus a fourth (tree and small building) in the painting's row of diminishing forms, drawn from the Hopi prophecy cave painting as orally told to the artist on the Peace Walk -- a full cycle of growth, disappearance, and return, not a one-way ascent.

World War One (2022), and by extension World War Two and Vietnam, mark the first documented return of the Art Collision 'unrepeated hybrid mode' — visible composited photograph and visible hand-worked paint coexisting on one surface — in over 20 years. Where Art Collision's digital compositing erased seams to create a false continuity that never existed, the Mediums of War paintings keep every photo-fragment discrete and legible: paint does the coherence-work that Photoshop once did, without hiding the seams. Recognized only now, through the archive process itself, not at time of making.

A confidence-and-transparency arc runs from Art Collision's seamless digital compositing (a younger, less confident Bernard, inclined to obscure) through World War One's visible-seam paint-compositing (increased confidence, showing the work rather than hiding it) to the archive's own radical transparency — raw unedited transcripts, honest-failure logging — as the fullest expression of that same growth. This is a process-dependent discovery visible only now, not a claim about original 2022 intent.

A personal fatalism traced to the Hopi prophecy heard at the Global Peace Walk (2000) resurfaces in World War One (2022) and is independently, unconsciously echoed in Walter Benjamin's writing on war as aesthetic spectacle. Logged as a coincidence/resonance across three unrelated paths — Peace Walk, painting, critical theory — not as a lineage.

Camera-awareness chain across the triptych: World War One's raw documentary photography teaches a generation to see itself historically. World War Two's subjects perform for that awareness (soldiers staging themselves for the camera, propagandists exploiting the same awareness to manufacture a moral narrative WWI never received). Vietnam's subjects are again not looking at the camera, but this is not a return to WWI's innocence — it is unawareness of a different mechanism (live, uncensored broadcast exposure) rather than unawareness that the camera would matter at all. Recognition, not present during painting.

The trust-economy across WWI, WWII, and Vietnam: WWII's manufactured 'good vs evil' narrative (built through propaganda apparatus on both sides, exemplified by the staged Khaldei Reichstag photograph) functions as capitalized moral credit for the US/West. Vietnam spends that credit down with a lag rather than starting from zero — the backfire of raw, uncensored Vietnam War footage was delayed by the size of the reserve built in the 1940s, and further diffused by the war spanning multiple US presidents rather than attaching to a single confirmed figure the way WWII attached to Hitler. The credit was badly dented (My Lai, the Pentagon Papers) but not exhausted, which is why the US was not rewritten as history's villain the way Nazi Germany was.

The Korea-gap: Korea (1950-53) is entirely absent from the Mediums of War project, chronologically sitting between WWII and Vietnam. Identified as technologically caused rather than thematically excluded: Korea falls in the gap between the recording media the project actually traces (still photography, color photography, 16mm sync-sound film) — the lightweight sync-sound cameras and broadcast infrastructure that defined Vietnam's media relationship weren't in place until deep into the 1960s. May be part of why Korea reads culturally as 'the forgotten war' more broadly, not just within this project.

Anachronism leaking across the medium-per-era scaffolding: The medium-per-era logic (b&w for WWI, color for WWII, film for Vietnam) is never as clean as the triptych's own scaffolding implies. Two WWII tanks appear as accidental anachronisms within the World War One painting (anachronism forward). At least four source images used in World War Two are modern digital colorizations of black-and-white originals rather than period color (anachronism backward) — undercutting the premise that color is WWII's native recording medium. Both read as the same underlying leak from opposite temporal directions.

Sourcing method as the mechanism enabling genuine discovery: Both World War One and World War Two began as tests (compositional test toward a larger format for WWI; a 'can I make this work with a bunch of photos' test for the sourcing method itself), with fast, near-random source selection rather than researched curation. This randomness is identified as the mechanism that makes the retrospective readings surfaced during cataloguing (Allied/German color-technology skew, named-vs-anonymous framing, cross-painting anachronism leaks) genuine discoveries rather than confirmations of an argument already quietly built in through deliberate curation — protecting the 'recognition not influence' principle at the sourcing level, not just the compositional level.

'World War Two' as retroactive bundling: The painting holds together three structurally distinct conflicts under one historical name: Finland's Continuation War against the USSR, the Pacific campaign against Japan, and the main European theater against Germany — fought by different belligerents for different reasons on largely separate timelines. Surfaced through a compositional pairing: Finnish soldiers displaying a captured Soviet map at Porlampi Motti (autumn 1941, cold) stacked above US Marines holding a handmade thank-you sign after Guam (1944, tropical heat) — structurally similar gestures (soldiers holding paper up for the camera) in unrelated theaters with no coordination between them, mirroring how the single name 'World War Two' bundles wars that likely didn't feel like one war to the people fighting them.

The anonymous witness figure as viewer-surrogate (Dürer descendant): A bust-portrait figure, cropped at the waist, floats impossibly in open water at the painting's left edge, gazing over the amphibious invasion scene — uncatalogued in the source list, deliberately left unidentified. Connects to two prior Dürer-derived devices already on record: the painting-within-painting self-insertion (After Turner, 1994) and the small-figure-in-vast-landscape convention, previously used as direct self-portraiture (Color Theory, 1995, the Goethe-reading figure). This figure evolves the device: not autobiographical, but a stand-in for any viewer — 'wearing the jersey of the good guys, but not really that invested,' costumed in allegiance without commitment, a generic viewer-surrogate for whoever happens to be looking, including future viewers of the archive itself, machine and human both.

Global Peace Walk 2000 as the shared root of Art Collision and Mediums of War: The Global Peace Walk 2000 (San Francisco to New York, events at American University and elsewhere in DC with Native spiritual leaders, arriving in New York for the UN's 55th anniversary) is already on record as Art Collision's philosophical turning point. Stated this session as also underlying Mediums of War, made twenty-plus years later: the same peace-oriented conviction turned toward a direct examination of war. Explicit stated intent: the paintings exist in part to make people 'look again and remember that we need peace.' Background: the walk followed the Nipponzan Myōhōji tradition of walks reenacting the Trail of Tears as meditation; a monk named Yamato, who participated in walks since the 1970s and in a 1995 walk, is recalled by the artist as involved, held as artist-remembered history without external documentation (the walk was deliberately low-media).
